prompt:
A teammate built a delete control as `
Delete
`. Keyboard users report that they cannot use it at all. What is the best fix?
explanation: Correct (native button): a `<button>` is focusable, runs its click handler on Enter and Space, is announced as a button and supports `disabled`, all for free. Wrong (tabindex="0"): the div can now be reached with Tab, but Enter and Space still do nothing and it is not announced as a button. Wrong (role="button"): screen readers now announce a button, but it still cannot be focused or activated from the keyboard, so it promises something it does not do. Wrong (keyboard shortcut): hidden and hard to discover, and the control itself is still unusable from the keyboard.
choices: Add a keyboard shortcut for deleting, and list that shortcut on the app's main help page
Add `tabindex="0"` to the div, so that keyboard users can reach it with the Tab key
Add `role="button"` to the div, so that screen readers announce it as a button
Use a native `<button type="button">`, which is focusable and works with Enter and Space

prompt: In a checkout form, each input has a visible `<span>` with its name ("Email", "Postal code") above it, and no other markup. Screen reader users hear only "edit text" when they move to each field. What is the best fix?
explanation: Correct (label with for/id): a `<label>` linked to the input gives it an accessible name that matches the visible text, so screen readers say "Email, edit text"; clicking the label also focuses the field, and voice-control users can say the name they see. Wrong (role="textbox"): inputs already have this role; the problem is the missing name, which this does not add. Wrong (title): some browsers use it as a last-resort name, but support is inconsistent and the tooltip is invisible to keyboard and touch users, so it is not a reliable fix. Wrong (aria-hidden on the span): it hides the only text there is and still leaves the input without a name.
choices: Change each `<span>` to a `<label>` whose `for` value matches the input's `id`
Add `role="textbox"` to each input, so that its purpose is announced to the user
Add a `title` attribute to each input, so that the name shows as a tooltip on hover
Add `aria-hidden="true"` to each `<span>`, so that the text is not read out twice

prompt: You are building a custom modal dialog for editing an address, without the native `<dialog>` element. Which focus behaviour is correct?
explanation: Correct: keyboard and screen reader users must land where the new content is; keeping Tab inside the dialog stops them reaching the covered page behind it; returning focus to the button that opened it puts them back where they were. (The native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` does most of this for you.) Wrong (keep focus on the opener): the user must Tab through the whole page to find the dialog, and screen readers are not told it opened. Wrong (close button, Tab continues behind): moving focus in is right, but letting Tab escape lets users act on hidden content behind the overlay. Wrong (blur): focus falls back to the page body, so users lose their place and nothing tells them a dialog opened.
choices: Keep focus on the button that opened it, so that users do not lose their place on the page
Move focus into the dialog, keep Tab inside it, and return focus to the opener on close
Move focus to the dialog's close button, and let Tab continue into the page behind it
Call `blur()` on the focused element, so screen readers start reading from the page top

prompt: In your single-page app, following a link replaces the page content without a full page load. Screen reader users say that nothing seems to happen when they follow a link, and they have to search for the new content. What is the best fix?
explanation: Correct: a client-side route change does not trigger the browser's normal "new page loaded" behaviour, so the app must do it: set `document.title` and move focus to the new main heading (made focusable with `tabindex="-1"`), or announce the new page title in a polite live region. Users then hear where they are and continue from the new content. Wrong (scroll to top): this only changes what sighted users see; screen reader focus stays on the old link. Wrong (assertive live region on main): it reads out the whole page on every change, including small updates, and interrupts whatever the user is doing. Wrong (role="navigation" on links): that role marks a group of navigation links as a landmark; putting it on each link is invalid and announces nothing about a page change.
choices: Add `aria-live="assertive"` to the whole main area, so every content change is read out
Scroll the window back to the top after each route change, so the new content is in view
After each route change, update the page title and move focus to the new main heading
Add `role="navigation"` to every link, so that following one is announced as a page change

prompt: A product page has three images: a photo of the product (a red running shoe), a decorative wavy line between two sections, and a magnifying-glass icon that is the only content of the search button. Which set of `alt` values is best?
explanation: Correct: the product photo carries information, so it is described; the decorative line gets an empty `alt` so screen readers skip it; the icon is the button's only content, so its `alt` names the action ("Search"), not its look. Wrong (describes the line and the magnifying glass): the decorative line adds noise, and "Magnifying glass" describes the picture instead of what the button does. Wrong (file name, missing alt): a file name tells the user nothing, and an image with no `alt` at all may be announced by its file name. Wrong (empty alt on the icon): the search button is left with no accessible name and is announced only as "button".
choices: Photo: `alt="Red running shoe, side view"`; line: `alt=""`; icon: `alt="Search"`
Photo: `alt="Red running shoe, side view"`; line: `alt="Wavy line"`; icon: `alt="Magnifying glass"`
Photo: `alt="shoe-red-01.jpg"`; line: no `alt` attribute; icon: `alt="Search"`
Photo: `alt="Red running shoe, side view"`; line: `alt=""`; icon: `alt=""`

prompt: Which of these uses of ARIA makes a page harder to use with a screen reader?
explanation: Correct: `aria-hidden` removes the sidebar from what screen readers see, but not from the Tab order, so keyboard focus lands on links that are announced as nothing or as blank. Hidden content should also be removed from the Tab order (for example with the `inert` attribute). Wrong (aria-label="Close"): this gives an icon-only button the name it needs. Wrong (aria-expanded): this tells users whether the menu is open, which is exactly what it is for. Wrong (aria-describedby): this makes the hint text be read after the field's name, which helps users.
choices: `aria-expanded` on a menu button, set to true or false as the menu opens and closes
`aria-label="Close"` on a button whose only content is an × icon
`aria-hidden="true"` on a sidebar that still contains links you can reach with Tab
`aria-describedby` on an input, pointing at the hint text "At least 8 characters"

prompt: A design uses grey body text at a normal size of 16px on a white background. Its contrast ratio is 3.2:1. A teammate says this passes WCAG 2 level AA. Which statement is correct?
explanation: Correct: WCAG 2 level AA asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal-size text, and 3:1 for large text (about 24px, or about 18.7px bold) and for the edges of controls and icons. 3.2:1 body text at 16px fails. Wrong (3:1 for all text): that is the large-text and non-text minimum, not the body-text one. Wrong (high-contrast mode): the page itself must meet the ratio; a user setting does not make the design pass. Wrong (7:1): that is the stricter AAA level, not AA.
choices: It passes, because WCAG level AA asks for a ratio of 3:1 for all of the text on a page
It fails, because normal-size text needs at least 4.5:1; 3:1 is only enough for large text
It passes, as long as users can switch their browser or system to a high-contrast mode
It fails, because WCAG level AA asks for 7:1 for body text, and 4.5:1 only for the headings

prompt: When a user clicks "Add to basket", a small message "Added to basket" appears near the button for three seconds. Focus stays on the button. Screen reader users hear nothing. Which approach announces the message reliably without interrupting the user?
explanation: Correct: screen readers announce changes to a live region they already know about. An empty `role="status"` region (which is polite) present from page load, whose text is then set, is announced after the user's current speech, without moving focus. Wrong (insert a new live region with the text): many screen readers do not announce a region that is added at the same moment as its content, because it was not registered before the change. Wrong (alert()): it does get read, but it is a blocking dialog that every user must dismiss, far too disruptive for a confirmation. Wrong (moving focus): it pulls keyboard users away from where they were working, and the message disappears after three seconds, leaving focus on nothing.
choices: Move focus to the message when it appears, and move focus back to the button afterwards
Insert a new element with `aria-live="polite"` and the message in it at the moment of the click
Show the message with the browser's `alert()` dialog, so that every screen reader reads it
Keep an empty `role="status"` element in the page from the start, and put the text into it

prompt: You are reviewing a pull request for a new navigation bar. Which of these changes make the page harder or impossible to use with a keyboard alone? Select all that apply.
choices: `:focus { outline: none; }` on all links, with no other focus style to replace it
Plain `<a href>` elements for links that go to other pages of the site
A submenu that opens only on mouse hover, with no way to open it from the keyboard
`tabindex="3"`, `"1"` and `"2"` on the first, second and third links, to set a custom Tab order
A focus ring styled with `:focus-visible`, so it shows for keyboard users only
explanation: Correct (outline: none with no replacement): keyboard users can no longer see where focus is. Correct (hover-only submenu): its links cannot be reached without a mouse. Correct (positive tabindex): Tab now visits the second, third and then first link, and all three before anything else on the page (a skip link or the logo included), so focus no longer follows the visual order; it also breaks as the page changes. DOM order should set the Tab order (WCAG 2.4.3; axe flags any tabindex above 0). Wrong (plain <a href>): native links are focusable and work with Enter, which is exactly right for navigation. Wrong (:focus-visible): it still shows a focus ring when the keyboard is used, and only hides it for mouse clicks.

prompt: A sign-up form shows validation errors after the user presses Submit. Which practices make the errors usable for screen reader users and for people who cannot tell red from green? Select all that apply.
choices: Show only a red border on each invalid field, so that the form's layout stays clean
Show an error text next to each invalid field, and link it with `aria-describedby`
Show the error message in a tooltip that appears when the mouse is over the field
After a failed submit, move focus to the first invalid field or to an error summary
Put the error message in the field's placeholder text, so that it is inside the field
Set `aria-invalid="true"` on each invalid field, and remove it once it is fixed
explanation: Correct (visible text linked with aria-describedby): the error does not rely on colour, and screen readers read it with the field. Correct (move focus after a failed submit): users are taken straight to the problem instead of having to search for it. Correct (aria-invalid): screen readers announce the field as invalid. Wrong (red border only): colour alone is invisible to many colour-blind users and says nothing to screen readers. Wrong (hover tooltip): keyboard, touch and screen reader users never trigger it. Wrong (placeholder): it disappears as soon as the user types, has weak contrast, and is not reliably announced as an error.

prompt: You need a gallery of product cards that fills as many equal-width columns as fit the screen. Cards must line up in neat rows and columns, including on the last, partly filled row. Which approach fits best?
explanation: Correct (Grid with auto-fill and minmax): Grid controls rows and columns together, so every card shares the same column tracks; `auto-fill` with `minmax` picks as many columns as fit, and cards on the last row keep the same width. Wrong (Flexbox with flex: 1): each wrapped line shares out its own space, so the cards on a partly filled last row stretch wider than the others and break the columns. Wrong (floats): always four columns whatever the screen size, plus old clearing hacks. Wrong (table): the cards are not tabular data, so the markup is wrong for screen readers, and it does not reflow on small screens.
choices: CSS Grid with `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr))`
Flexbox with `flex-wrap: wrap` and `flex: 1` on each card, so cards stretch to fill rows
Floats with `width: 25%` on each card, and a clearfix on the gallery container
An HTML `<table>` with four columns that scrolls sideways on narrow screens

prompt: A UI library's stylesheet contains `#app .nav a { color: blue; }`. Your own stylesheet loads after it and contains `.button { color: white; }`. A link `<a class="button">` inside the nav is still blue. Why?
explanation: Correct: `#app .nav a` has one id, one class and one element, which beats a single class. Source order only decides between rules of equal specificity. Fixes include matching or raising the specificity, putting the library in a lower `@layer`, or avoiding ids in selectors. Wrong (third-party always wins): both files are ordinary page stylesheets; neither gets priority for where it came from. Wrong (duplicate skipped): a later rule is never ignored; at equal specificity it would win. Wrong (only :link): page styles on `a` elements work fine; `:link` just matches links that have not been visited.
choices: Link colours are set by the browser, and they can only be changed with the `:link` selector
Rules from third-party stylesheets always win over your own rules unless you use `!important`
Your rule loads later, so the browser treats it as a duplicate of the earlier rule and skips it
The library selector contains an id, so it is more specific and wins although it comes first

prompt: A dropdown menu has `position: absolute; z-index: 9999`, but it appears behind the page header, which has `position: sticky; z-index: 10`. The dropdown sits inside a card that has `transform: translateY(0)` (left over from an animation) and no z-index. What is the cause?
explanation: Correct: a transform (like opacity below 1, `filter`, or a positioned element with a z-index) makes the card a stacking context. The dropdown's 9999 is only compared with things inside the card; the card as a whole is painted at level 0, below the header's 10. Fixes: remove the leftover transform, give the card a stacking order above the header, or render the dropdown outside the card (a portal). Wrong (no effect on absolute): z-index works on any positioned element, absolute included. Wrong (sticky always on top): sticky elements follow the same z-index rules as other positioned elements. Wrong (same parent): elements anywhere in the same stacking context can be ordered; the real limit is the stacking context, not the parent.
choices: The card's `transform` creates a new stacking context, so 9999 only counts inside the card
`z-index` has no effect on elements with `position: absolute`, only on ones that are `relative`
Sticky elements are always painted above absolute ones, whatever their z-index is
`z-index` only works between elements that share the same direct parent element

prompt: A product card component appears both in a wide main column and in a narrow sidebar on the same page. It should stack its image above its text whenever the card itself is narrower than 400px. Which approach fits best?
explanation: Correct: a container query (with `container-type: inline-size` on the wrapper) reacts to the space the card actually has, so the same component stacks in the sidebar and stays side by side in the main column. Wrong (media query): it tests the viewport width; on a wide screen the sidebar card is narrow but the query never matches. Wrong (vw units): they also follow the viewport, not the card. Wrong (window resize listener): it also only knows the window size, adds JavaScript work on every resize, and does not run when the column changes width for other reasons (for example a sidebar being opened).
choices: Image and text widths in `vw` units, so that they shrink with the browser window
A media query such as `@media (max-width: 400px)` around the stacked layout rules
A container query on the card's wrapper, such as `@container (max-width: 400px)`
A listener on the window's `resize` event that adds a class to every card on the page

prompt: An element has `width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 2px solid gray;` and no `box-sizing` rule, so the browser default applies. It overflows its 300px-wide column. How wide is it on screen?
explanation: Correct (344px): the default `box-sizing: content-box` applies `width` to the content only, then adds padding and border on both sides: 300 + 2 × 20 + 2 × 2 = 344. With `box-sizing: border-box` it would be exactly 300px, which is why many projects set it globally. Wrong (300px): that is the border-box result. Wrong (322px): adds the padding and border for one side only. Wrong (340px): adds the padding but forgets the border.
choices: 340px
300px
322px
344px

prompt: You add `position: sticky; top: 0;` to a table's header row so that it stays visible while the page scrolls. Instead, it scrolls away with the rest of the table. Which cause is most likely?
explanation: Correct: a sticky element sticks to its nearest ancestor that has an `overflow` other than `visible`. A common case is a wrapper with `overflow-x: auto` for wide tables; that wrapper does not scroll vertically itself, so the header never sticks to the page. Fix it by removing that overflow, or by making the wrapper the vertical scroll area (with a height limit). Wrong (z-index): z-index only decides what paints on top; it does not turn sticking on. Wrong (parent needs position: relative): sticky does not need a positioned parent; that rule belongs to `position: absolute`. Wrong (fixed height): sticky has no height requirement.
choices: A parent has `overflow: hidden` or `auto`, so the header sticks only within that box
Sticky positioning only works when the element also has a `z-index` value set
Sticky positioning only works when the parent element has `position: relative` set
Sticky positioning only works on elements that have a fixed height set in pixels

prompt: A notification slides in at the top of the page by animating its `margin-top` from -60px to 0. While it animates, the content below is pushed down, the page records layout shifts, and the animation stutters on low-end phones. What is the best fix?
explanation: Correct: with `position: fixed` the notification no longer takes up space, so nothing else moves, and a `transform` is applied after layout, without recalculating it, so the animation is smooth and is not counted as a layout shift. Wrong (will-change: margin-top): a margin change still needs a new layout on every frame and still pushes the content. Wrong (setInterval every 16 ms): still a layout on every step, and timers are not in step with the screen's frames, so it stutters more. Wrong (animate a spacer's height): the content below still moves on every frame, which is the same shift.
choices: Add `will-change: margin-top`, so that the browser can prepare the margin animation in advance
Take it out of the page flow with `position: fixed`, and animate `transform: translateY()` instead
Animate `margin-top` from JavaScript with `setInterval` every 16 ms, for smaller and smoother steps
Animate the `height` of an empty spacer above the content instead, so the notification stays still

prompt: A full-screen mobile menu uses `height: 100vh`. On phones, the buttons at the bottom of the menu are hidden behind the browser's address bar and toolbar. What is the best fix?
explanation: Correct: on mobile browsers `vh` is based on the largest viewport (with the browser bars hidden), so `100vh` is taller than the visible area while the bars show. `dvh` (dynamic viewport height) follows the area that is actually visible; `svh` uses the smallest. Wrong (100vw): it is based on the width, which has nothing to do with the bars. Wrong (100% without parent heights): a percentage height needs a parent with a set height, otherwise it behaves like `auto`. Wrong (overflow: hidden on body): it stops the page scrolling, but the menu is still taller than the visible area, so its bottom buttons stay out of reach.
choices: Use `height: 100vw`, so that the height is taken from the width of the phone's screen instead
Use `height: 100dvh`, which follows the visible area as the browser bars appear and hide
Use `height: 100%` on the menu, without setting any height on its parent elements
Add `overflow: hidden` to the body, so that the page behind the menu cannot scroll

prompt: A flex row has a text column with `flex: 1` and a fixed-width Delete button. When the text column shows a long file name with no spaces, the column will not shrink, the content overflows the screen and the button is pushed out of view. Which changes fix this? Select all that apply.
choices: Set `flex-shrink: 1` on the text column, so that it is allowed to become narrower
Set `min-width: 0` on the text column, and add `overflow-wrap: anywhere` to the name
Give the Delete button a higher `z-index`, so that it is painted on top of the text
Set `overflow: hidden` and `text-overflow: ellipsis` on the text column
Set `width: 100%` on the flex container, so its content cannot be wider than the screen
explanation: Background: a flex item has `min-width: auto` by default, so it will not shrink below its content's minimum width, here the whole unbroken file name. Correct (min-width: 0 plus overflow-wrap: anywhere): the column may now shrink, and the long name breaks onto several lines inside it. Correct (overflow: hidden with an ellipsis): an item whose overflow is not `visible` gets a minimum width of 0, so it shrinks and the name is cut off with "…". Wrong (flex-shrink: 1): `flex: 1` already sets it; the minimum width is what stops the shrinking. Wrong (z-index): the button is outside the visible area, and painting order cannot bring it back. Wrong (width: 100% on the container): the container is already as wide as its parent; the item overflows the container, it does not make the container grow.

prompt: A user with low vision changes their browser's default font size from 16px to 24px (in the browser settings, not with page zoom). Which `font-size` values for your body text will grow with this setting? Select all that apply.
choices: `16px` on the body text
`2vw` on the body text
`1rem` on the body text
`calc(12px + 0.5vw)` on the body text
`112.5%` on the `html` element, with body text inheriting it
explanation: Correct (1rem): rem is relative to the root font size, which starts at the user's chosen default, so 1rem becomes 24px. Correct (112.5% on html): a percentage on the root scales the user's default, giving 27px, and everything sized in rem or em follows. Wrong (16px): a pixel value ignores the default font size setting (only page zoom scales it). Wrong (2vw): it follows the window width, not the user's font setting. Wrong (calc(12px + 0.5vw)): made only of pixels and viewport units, so the setting has no effect on it.

prompt: A comments component renders each comment as raw HTML (with React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, or `v-html` in Vue) so that line breaks and links display nicely. A tester posts the comment below, and it runs in the browser of every visitor who opens the page: ```html ``` What is the best fix?
explanation: Correct: rendering the comment as text lets the framework escape it, so markup is shown, not run. If some formatting is needed, an allow-list sanitiser such as DOMPurify removes event handlers, `javascript:` links and other dangerous markup. Wrong (strip <script> with a regex): this payload has no script tag at all; event-handler attributes, SVG and many encodings get past home-made filters. Wrong (browser-side check): an attacker sends the comment straight to the API and skips your form entirely. Wrong (Secure flag): it only stops the cookie being sent over plain HTTP; scripts can still read it (that is what HttpOnly prevents), and injected script can do anything the user can do anyway.
choices: Remove every `<script>` tag from each comment with a regular expression before it is rendered
Render the comment as plain text, or clean the HTML with a proven sanitiser such as DOMPurify
Check in the browser that the comment contains no `<` character before it is submitted
Set the `Secure` flag on all cookies, so that `document.cookie` cannot be sent elsewhere

prompt: Your site sends the header `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'`. An attacker finds a bug that lets them inject `<script>alert(1)</script>` or an `onerror="..."` attribute into one of your pages. What does the header do?
explanation: Correct: CSP is enforced by the browser. `script-src 'self'` (without `'unsafe-inline'`) blocks inline `<script>` blocks, inline event-handler attributes and scripts loaded from other hosts, so this payload does not run. It is a second line of defence: the injection bug still has to be fixed, because injected HTML can still change the page and a script hosted on your own origin would still be allowed. Wrong (server strips HTML): CSP does not change response bodies; it only tells the browser what it may load and run. Wrong (iframes): that is the `frame-ancestors` directive, which protects against clickjacking. Wrong (blocks other origins calling your API): that confuses CSP with CORS; `script-src` says nothing about who may call your API.
choices: The web server strips the injected HTML out of every response before it is sent to users
The browser will not run inline scripts or scripts from other sites, so the payload is blocked
Other websites can no longer load your pages inside an iframe, which stops this attack
The browser blocks all requests from other origins to your API, so stolen data cannot be sent out

prompt: Your app's session cookie is set with `SameSite=None; Secure`, because the app must also work inside a partner's website in an iframe. The endpoint `POST /api/transfer` moves money. Which defence stops other websites from forging this request?
explanation: Correct: with `SameSite=None` the browser attaches the cookie to requests started by any site, so the server needs proof that the request came from your own page. A CSRF token that your page reads and sends back gives that proof, because other sites cannot read your pages to learn it (checking the `Origin` header is a useful extra check). Wrong (rely on CORS): CORS only decides whether the other site's script may read the response; a cross-site form post or simple request is still sent with the cookie, and the transfer still happens. Wrong (HttpOnly): it stops scripts reading the cookie, but the browser still attaches it to forged requests. Wrong (POST only): another site can submit a hidden form with `method="post"` to your API.
choices: Require a CSRF token that your page sends in a header and the server checks on every change
Rely on CORS: since the API does not allow other origins, their requests never reach your server
Mark the session cookie `HttpOnly`, so that other sites are unable to use it in their own requests
Accept only POST for changes, because other sites can only send GET requests to your API

prompt: A React app calls a paid third-party API directly from the browser. The secret API key is stored in `.env` as `VITE_PAYMENTS_SECRET` and read in the app's code with `import.meta.env.VITE_PAYMENTS_SECRET`. The `.env` file is listed in `.gitignore`. Is the key safe?
explanation: Correct: values the client code reads from `import.meta.env` (and similar `REACT_APP_` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variables) are written into the bundle as plain strings at build time, and the key is also visible in every request the browser sends. The browser should call your own server, which holds the key and calls the third-party API. Wrong (.gitignore): it keeps the file out of Git, not out of the built JavaScript. Wrong (minified): minifying renames variables but leaves string values as they are. Wrong (only source maps): the key is in the minified code itself, so removing source maps changes nothing.
choices: Yes, as long as the production bundle is minified, which makes the key very hard to find
Yes: `.env` is in `.gitignore`, so the value never leaves the machines that build the app
No: the build copies the value into the JavaScript every visitor downloads; keep it on a server
No, but only because of source maps; turning them off in production keeps the key hidden

prompt: Marketing wants a third-party chat widget on every page, including checkout, added with `<script src="https://widget.vendor.example/chat.js"></script>`. Which of these are real risks of doing this? Select all that apply.
choices: The script runs with full access to the page, so it can read what users type into the card form
If the vendor's server is hacked, the attacker's code runs on your site for every visitor
The script can read your server's environment variables, such as the database password
The script can read cookies marked HttpOnly and send them to the vendor's own server
If the vendor's server is slow or down, it can delay or break the loading of your page
explanation: Correct (full page access): a script included this way runs with the same rights as your own code, so it can read form fields, including card details. Correct (vendor compromise): you run whatever that URL serves at the moment, so a hacked vendor means hacked checkout pages (keep such scripts off payment pages, pin versions with Subresource Integrity where possible, and limit sources with CSP). Correct (slow or down vendor): a blocking script in the page waits for the vendor's server, and its errors can break your page. Wrong (server environment variables): code in the browser cannot reach your server's environment. Wrong (HttpOnly cookies): no page script, yours or theirs, can read HttpOnly cookies.

prompt: Which of these can any signed-in user of your public web app see, using only the browser's developer tools? Select all that apply.
choices: Environment variables on the API server that the client-side code never references
Every field in the API's JSON responses to them, including fields the UI never shows
Your original, unminified source code, if source map files are published with the site
Records that the API returns only to admins, after it checks the caller's role
The code of admin-only screens, if it is bundled into the JavaScript every user loads
explanation: Rule: anything sent to the browser is visible to its user. Correct (hidden JSON fields): the network tab shows the full response, so the API should only send fields the user may see. Correct (published source maps): they rebuild the original files, comments included. Correct (bundled admin code): code in the bundle can be read by anyone who loads it; this is fine only if the API, not the hidden screen, enforces who may do what. Wrong (server environment variables): they never reach the browser unless code sends them. Wrong (admin-only records): if the server checks the role, these records are never sent to a normal user.

prompt: In a component test written with Testing Library, which way of finding the form's Submit button follows the library's guidance best, and also checks that the button is accessible?
explanation: Correct: `getByRole` finds elements the way users and assistive technology do, by role and accessible name, so the test fails if the button becomes a div or loses its name, and it survives changes to classes and markup. Wrong (querySelector on a class): it ties the test to CSS class names that users never see and that change during refactors. Wrong (getByTestId): an escape hatch for when nothing else works; it checks nothing about what users see or hear. Wrong (getByText): it finds the text, but a div that says "Submit" would pass even though it is not a working button.

prompt: A search box waits until the user has stopped typing for 300 ms, then calls the API. explanation: Correct: fake timers (for example `vi.useFakeTimers()` in Vitest or `jest.useFakeTimers()` in Jest) replace the real clock, so the test moves time forward exactly and instantly; the 299 ms and 300 ms checks give the same result on every run and the test takes no real time. Wrong (real timers): the test's timer and the component's timer are only 1 ms apart, and timers can fire late on a busy machine, so the two checks are unreliable, and every such test is slow. Wrong (0 ms delay under test): a test-only code path means the 300 ms behaviour is never tested at all. Wrong (retrying assertion): it only proves that a request is sent at some point within 2 seconds; it cannot show that nothing was sent at 299 ms or that the delay is 300 ms.

Set the delay to 0 ms when the code runs under test, so the test does not have to wait for anything
Use the test runner's fake timers: advance the clock by 299 ms and check, then by 1 ms more and check
Use a retrying assertion that waits up to 2 seconds until exactly one request has been sent

Wrong (no minification): larger, slower downloads for every user, and bundling still merges files, so original files and lines are still lost. explanation: Automated checkers test the rendered page against rules a program can decide. Correct (no alt attribute): whether the attribute exists is a simple check (axe rule image-alt). Correct (input with no name): the tool computes each field's accessible name and reports an empty one (axe rule label). Correct (2.5:1 contrast on a plain background): the tool reads both colours in the real browser and computes the ratio (axe rule color-contrast; this is why the item says real browser, since jsdom-based component tests switch this rule off). Wrong (wrong alt text): the tool sees that alt text exists but cannot judge whether it describes the image. Wrong (focus not returned): this is behaviour over time, after a user action, which a static scan of the page does not exercise. Wrong (dropdown ignores arrow keys): the tool can check roles and attributes, not how the widget responds to keys. These need manual keyboard and screen reader testing; automated tools find only part of real accessibility problems.
